correctness.rationale: For P(z)=1-(3/2)z+3z²+2z³, exactly independently expanded |P(re^{iθ})|² as a degree-three polynomial Q(r,x), x=cosθ. At r=1 it equals 81/4-16(1-x)(x+1/2)²; hence global maxima only x=1, x=-1/2, with one axis and one conjugate pair. Direct exact differentiation gives Q_x(1,1)=36>0, Q_xx(1,-1/2)=-48<0 and radial height difference slope 27>0. A compact annulus and analytic implicit-function theorem preserve those nondegenerate peaks, exclude every other global maximum, and guarantee a unique transverse crossing under small real-symmetric C³ perturbations. Inductively H_j(z)=R_j^-m_j/2 z^m_j P(z/R_j), m_j=2deg(F_{j-1})+10, dominates earlier polynomial on its new large-radius annulus because m_j/2>deg(F_{j-1}), yet tends to zero with derivatives on all old compacts. Finitely many inequalities per stage and summable future-perturbation budgets preserve every prior crossing. The disjoint coefficient blocks have log(1/|a_n|)>=(m_j/2)j log(m_j+3)-O(1) when R_j>=(m_j+3)^j, giving entire order zero via the coefficient criterion, while infinitely many nonzero blocks guarantee transcendence. A separate exact SymPy expansion confirmed seed identity, derivatives and 27; the finite verifier cannot prove this infinite induction.

value.rationale: The number of global maximum-modulus points is a natural invariant in the Erdős/Hayman maximum-modulus problem. Demonstrating infinitely many genuinely transverse triple exceptions at growth order zero and first nonzero coefficient gap one distinguishes exceptional circles from generic-count restrictions, and is not a routine restatement of finite polynomial examples. It does not claim the separate component-theoretic discontinuity problem.

limitations: Exception radii are recursively selected, not prescribed; no density or effective exhaustive sequence is asserted.
Transverse switching of local maximum branches does not automatically prove a discontinuity of the connected maximum-modulus set.
The first Taylor gap is one, while the exceptional radii are locally finite as demanded by Li's theorem.
